meta.title: The Electrode Budget
meta.subtitle: How much EEG accuracy survives when a lab cap becomes a wearable?

tasks.name: Imagine moving a hand
tasks.person: A cue appears. Without moving, the participant imagines opening and closing the left or right hand for four seconds.
tasks.computer: The decoder looks for a drop in the 8–13 Hz mu rhythm over the motor cortex, on the side opposite the imagined hand.
tasks.why: The classic brain–computer interface task, and the cleanest test of placement: the signal is focal, so a small sensorimotor patch should beat electrodes spread evenly over the head.
tasks.headline: Eight electrodes over the motor cortex keep about 91% of full-cap accuracy.
tasks.signalCaption: C3 and C4 sit over the left and right motor cortex. The ~10 Hz wiggle is the mu rhythm the decoder uses; it drops over the hand being imagined.

tasks.name: Spot the target
tasks.person: Letters or icons flash one at a time. The participant silently counts the flashes that contain the target.
tasks.computer: A rare target flash produces a positive voltage bump about 300–500 ms later — the P300 — which xDAWN + Riemannian decoding picks up.
tasks.why: P300 is a slow, widespread response, so this is the case where a headband-sized montage has a real chance. The cap is already only eight electrodes.
tasks.headline: Half the electrodes still keep about 95% of P300 performance.
tasks.signalCaption: Averaged at Pz. The target (teal) has a clear positive bump around 400 ms; standard flashes (gray) do not.

tasks.name: Stare at a flicker
tasks.person: The participant looks at one of twelve targets. Each target flickers at a different fixed frequency.
tasks.computer: The visual cortex echoes the flicker. A CCA decoder reads the frequency from the occipital EEG and reports which target was chosen.
tasks.why: SSVEP is fast and accuracy-scored, so it can be summarized as information transfer rate (bits/min) — the metric that decides whether a wearable BCI is actually usable.
tasks.headline: Four occipital electrodes keep 98% of full-cap accuracy and 43 of 44.5 bits/min.
tasks.signalTitle: The flicker shows up in the spectrum
tasks.signalCaption: Occipital EEG while one target flickers at 13.75 Hz. The peak at the flicker frequency and its harmonic is the signature the decoder reads.

tasks.name: Clench a fist
tasks.person: On cue, the participant clenches the left or right fist. EEG is recorded at the same time from a dense scalp cap and eight in-ear electrodes.
tasks.computer: The decoder tries to tell left from right. On the scalp, motor cortex carries the signal; in the ear, the same movement is much harder to read.
tasks.why: The only dataset here where the same person, in the same session, has both a dense cap and a wearable. It separates electrode site from channel count.
tasks.headline: At the same eight channels, scalp scores 0.739 and in-ear scores 0.464.
tasks.signalTitle: One electrode, left vs right fist
tasks.signalCaption: Single-channel beta-band AUC, averaged over subjects. On this averaged view the best scalp electrode is above chance and the best ear electrode is not; individual ear channels do cross chance in some subjects, so the montage-level comparison at matched channel count is the reported result.

tasks.name: Score a night’s sleep
tasks.person: The participant sleeps at home wearing scalp and ear electrodes. Each 30-second window is scored as Wake, REM, N1, N2 or N3.
tasks.computer: A simple band-power + LDA model predicts the stage from each window. Scoring uses Cohen’s κ, where zero is chance.
tasks.why: Sleep is the wearable-native continuous task. Unlike a focal motor rhythm, slow sleep waves are broad, so the ear has a better chance.
tasks.headline: The ear is close, not equal: −0.056 κ at matched six channels.
tasks.signalCaption: Hypnogram from subject 001. The model sees only 30-second windows; the benchmark asks how well it recovers this sequence from scalp vs ear electrodes.

tasks.name: Sit still, then multitask
tasks.person: The participant sits quietly for two and a half minutes, then works through the SIMKAP multitasking test for two and a half minutes, wearing a 14-channel Emotiv EPOC.
tasks.computer: Band power in four bands per 4-second window, classified by shrinkage LDA. The decoder has to tell a resting recording from a multitasking one.
tasks.why: The largest cohort here (48 people) and the only headset rather than cap, so it is the one place where a frontal “glasses-like” four-electrode subset can be measured against a full montage. Its four-electrode sets are scalp proxies, labelled as such, not measured glasses hardware.
tasks.headline: Four frontal electrodes keep 97% of the 14-channel score.
tasks.signalCaption: AF3 from subject 01: the resting recording, then the first ten seconds of the SIMKAP task. The task recording carries more high-frequency muscle activity and a weaker alpha rhythm — part of what the decoder is reading.

tasks.name: Follow one voice
tasks.person: Two talkers speak at once. The participant attends to one of them while scalp, around-ear and in-ear EEG are recorded at the same time.
tasks.computer: A ridge decoder reconstructs the attended speech envelope from EEG, and the talker whose envelope correlates more with the reconstruction wins. Decisions are made on 60 s windows, the paper's headline length.
tasks.why: The only public dataset that records all three systems simultaneously, so it is a direct test of the ear site for this paradigm rather than a geometric proxy. It is also the task where the ear costs the most.
tasks.headline: At twelve electrodes each, the in-ear set keeps 78% of the matched scalp score.
tasks.signalCaption: Correlation between the reconstructed and the true attended envelope, per subject, for the scalp cap and the in-ear set. The scalp decoder tracks the speech envelope; the in-ear decoder tracks it less.

tasks.name: Imagine a hand, a foot or a tongue
tasks.person: The same nine people and the same cap as the two-class task, but four cues: left hand, right hand, both feet, tongue.
tasks.computer: Same decoder, same montages, four classes instead of two. Feet and tongue are represented near the midline, so a lateralised sensorimotor patch has less to work with.
tasks.why: Class count is an axis the rest of the benchmark holds fixed. If the cost of a small montage grows when you ask it to distinguish more things, then 'eight electrodes are enough' is only true for the two-class version of a task.
tasks.headline: The same eight sensorimotor electrodes keep 91% of a two-class score but only 85% of a four-class one.
tasks.signalCaption: C3 and C4 sit over the left and right motor cortex. The ~10 Hz wiggle is the mu rhythm the decoder uses; it drops over the hand being imagined. The four-class task adds feet and tongue, which are not lateralised.

tasks.name: Watch a video, read the mood
tasks.person: The participant watches short videos chosen to elicit a particular emotion, while 30 scalp electrodes record.
tasks.computer: Band power in four bands per 4-second window, classified as positive or negative valence. A video gets one prediction, averaged over its windows.
tasks.why: The largest cohort here by a wide margin (123 people) and the only affect task. It is also the one where the wearable question is asked of a frontal site, and where the answer is uncomfortably small: the effect is only about six points above chance to begin with.
tasks.headline: Four posterior electrodes keep 98% of a 30-channel score that is itself only six points above chance.
tasks.signalCaption: Band power at four electrodes, averaged over participants, for the two valence classes. The separation is small and it is not where a glasses frame would put its electrodes.

comparisons.title: Same eight channels, same session
comparisons.note: Negative in 6/6 subjects; paired 95% CI [−0.378, −0.173] AUC. Same session, same eight channels, same decoder.

comparisons.title: Matched six channels, nine nights
comparisons.note: Negative in 9/9 nights; paired 95% CI [−0.104, −0.009] κ.

positionNote: Scalp positions are standard 10-5 locations projected top-down. Ear positions are schematic; they are not part of the 10-5 nomenclature.
